date: 11 September 2026 JST · Lemma F pole-angle proof
title: The selected-net theorem is proved for sharpest curvature at least 180°
body:
The new geometric proof excludes a finite-cut crossing by trapping a neighboring patch in a triangle where its apex cannot fit. The spherical-link bound makes the needed pole angles acute whenever the sharpest curvature is at least 180°, including equality. The selected net then has all 28 pairs safe.

Below 180°, nonobtuse original or flattened pole angles still suffice. A second circle argument handles obtuse original angles when the blue angle plus gap is at least 90°. The remaining target requires both angles obtuse and a gap-crossing angle below 90°. Its joint realizability is not established.

Four exact examples, including an 18-coordinate box and an obtuse example repaired by the circle argument, agree with independent all-28 certificates. The general selected rule, the every-slit Lemma F, the full octahedron, and n=6 remain open. These are geometric subfamilies, not a percentage of shape space.

date: 11 September 2026 JST · Case B cut-entry proof
title: The fan route is excluded; the common-direction pattern leaves one segment
body:
The new theorem makes whole-net safety equivalent to two finite radial cut segments missing their remote petals. The through-fan bound from Lemma L excludes reaching those segments through the fan. Only entry across the slit gap remains.

This proves new subcases even when the slit-side endpoint passes X: convex remote patches, leans away from the gap, and leans with insufficient angular reach. When all inward patches lean the same way, one of the two segment checks is automatic. The remaining common-direction three-patch family therefore leaves one check.

The general angular bound and finite-edge separation remain open. The unconditional count stays 22/28; no completion percentage is inferred. Exact replays of four saved examples, including 11- and 18-coordinate boxes, agree with their independent all-28 certificates. Numerical searches are exploratory only.

title: Six far-pair checks reduced to two direct cut-side tests
body:
The new geometric reduction uses the completed Lemma L: if the two distant petals avoid the blue triangles beside the slit, the opposite petals are safe, then the interior blue targets are safe. It reverses the direction of the old refuted reduction and retains the troublesome cut boundary explicitly.

In the small-angle branch, the slit-side far endpoint at or before X is now proved safe even when the other far endpoint passes X. The slit-side-past-X branch remains open. The same two tests also need study outside the small-angle branch.

The count stays 22/28 unconditional pairs, but only two direct checks suffice for the other six. Exact two-pair certificates on four saved examples, including 11- and 18-coordinate boxes, agree with independent all-28 certificates. The full octahedron and n=6 remain open; numerical experiments are not proof premises.

title: All three local pairs proved: both overlap routes are closed
body:
The complete geometric proof of Lemma L now settles all three local pairs. First the cut-edge separator closed the entire below-180° branch, including the old angular counterexample. Then a spherical-link bound and a cosine-law comparison excluded the through-fan route for every curvature sum under the pole comparison.

The one-extending-patch and two-extending-patch cases are both proved, with equality and straight corners included. No numerical search is a proof premise. The current count changes from 0/3 to 3/3 universal local pairs, and from 19/28 to 22/28 safe pairs in the selected net.

The remaining work is in Lemma F: opposite petals in their small-fan-angle branch, then the cut-side far-fan pairs. The full octahedron and n=6 remain open. The four-opening class record has not been recounted, and its 2/47 figures are separate. Earlier entries remain below as historical progress states.

date: 10 September 2026 JST · Lemma L curvature split
title: A direct partial proof for Lemma L: separate the two possible overlap routes
body:
The new geometric proof compares the slit vertex’s curvature plus the fan center’s curvature with 180°. At or below this value it excludes meeting through the intervening fan; at or above it excludes meeting across the slit. At equality all three local pairs are safe. Explicit corner conditions prove additional local families.

Below 180°, a remaining overlap must involve the unique petal inward at the slit. Its two targets are the other petal and the other fan face; the third local pair is already safe in that subcase. An exact 18-coordinate box around the earlier angular counterexample retains both selection rules and proves a 6/5 radial separation ratio. All 28 face pairs pass independent certificates throughout the box.

Both strict halves remain open in general. The count stays 0 of 3 universal local obligations, 4 of 5 entire patch regimes, and 2 excluded / 47 open fixed-source classes. The displayed three-patch solid is the earlier uncovered example with a different fifth cut, not a proof of its entire family. Earlier progress entries remain below.

title: A proved four-tree rule inside the last three-patch pattern
body:
The middle-patch theorem proves common-direction three-patch subfamilies. A simple condition compares the middle inward-angle excess with the smaller pole curvature. A stronger version separately bounds the two middle extensions and uses curvature at the first inward vertex. Both give four prescribed trees and a written pole-switching proof.

Exact point examples and an 18-coordinate region pass the hypotheses and all 28 independent face-pair checks. They fail the older weighted-curvature criterion for all three opposite pairs. An exact uncovered example fails a middle-gap condition but still unfolds.

The remaining hypotheses split into two precise branches. The whole three-patch pattern is not settled, so the coarse count stays 4 of 5 entire regimes, with the fifth partly proved. The original fixed-source count stays 2 excluded and 47 open. No numerical survey is used as a proof.

title: Both two-patch arrangements proved; three mixed directions are covered too
body:
The new geometric proof uses an exact identity: a patch’s extensions viewed from the two poles sum to its reflex excess. Summing over the bad patches gives a shared angle budget when all vertex curvatures are below 180°. A larger-curvature pole supplies the complementary case.

This settles adjacent and opposite two-patch configurations under H. It also settles three bad patches with mixed directions. The three patches all leaning the same way are the remaining pattern.

The coarse existence count changes from 2 of 5 regimes to 4 of 5, with the fifth partly settled. This is not a coverage percentage. The four-cut source may change, so the original fixed-source target remains 2 excluded and 47 open. The full octahedron remains open.

Exact coordinates and an 18-coordinate region independently verify the hypotheses and every face pair of the saved nets. The universal claims come from the written identities and case proofs, not numerical surveys.

title: One bad patch: a complete existence proof by exchanging the poles
body:
The two-pole proof settles existence for the entire one-nonconvex-patch family when a pole is globally sharpest. Both prescribed trees use the same equator endpoint for the fifth cut. If both whole-patch cone tests failed, an equator vertex would have curvature above 180° while both poles had curvature below 180°, contradicting sharpness.

The half-turn fan proof also handles all three possible direction patterns of two adjacent bad patches when either pole has curvature at least 180°. Exact examples and an 18-coordinate region have independent all-pairs checks.

The old fixed sharpest-source claim remains open, and the 49-class count stays 2 excluded and 47 open. The new existence theorem does not rely on the refuted far-fan reduction. These families can overlap older sufficient criteria; no coverage percentage is inferred.

title: A supporting lemma fails; independent curvature and sector proofs survive
body:
An exact convex octahedron has one far-fan overlap and all other 27 pairs safe. Its source is not sharpest, so the proposed sharpest-source rule is not refuted. The old unrestricted reduction is false.

The current rigorous target is 49 classes, 2 excluded and 47 open. The one-patch whole-net argument has a remaining step. The new curvature theorem still proves every centrally symmetric octahedron, and a stronger local sector test certifies further asymmetric families.

A further proved reduction puts every vertex of curvature at least 120° on one face whenever the opposite-pair theorem fails. The remaining one-, two-, and three-high-vertex branches are all open in full.

The corrected interior-fan lemma leaves only two slit-side far-fan pairs once local and opposite-petal safety are known. The all-convex-patch proof also gives a simple complete family: all octahedra with nonobtuse triangular faces.

title: An opposite-pair curvature test; every centrally symmetric octahedron follows
body:
Later correction: the boundary audit withdraws the 24-class reduction and one-patch whole-net claim recorded in this historical entry.

The curvature-pair proof guarantees a net if the sharper pole’s curvature plus twice its opposite’s is at least 360°. The required short edge follows by adding two elementary triangle-angle comparisons. This proves every centrally symmetric octahedron.

A separate short-edge condition proves further geometric families, including some shapes with three nonconvex patches. Both arguments use the exterior-sector star-unfolding theorem. Their conditions are not universal. The fixed-source class count remains 2 excluded and 22 open, and no additional whole six-vertex type has been settled.

title: Two geometric regimes proved; a second failure class excluded
body:
Later correction: the boundary audit withdraws the 24-class reduction and one-patch whole-net claim recorded in this historical entry.

The new patch analysis proves unfoldability for all shapes with zero or one nonconvex blue–orange patch, with the sharpest-apex hypothesis in the one-patch case. It also proves that four nonconvex patches are impossible, excluding original class 20.

Two of the 24 sufficient failure classes are now excluded; 22 remain. The two-adjacent, two-opposite, and three-patch regimes remain open. Five exact examples check that the regimes occur, independently of the universal written proofs. No additional whole six-vertex type is settled.

title: Two switching implications proved; 23 sufficient failure classes remain
body:
Later correction: the boundary audit withdraws the 24-class reduction and one-patch whole-net claim recorded in this historical entry.

The new case analysis follows the proposal to assume an overlap and study another opening. Moving the opening repairs all three old local pairs. For opposite petals, the two route-angle sums add to 360° plus the deficit at w, so under the sharpest-apex hypothesis the same petals cannot overlap along both routes.

Reusing the conditional hinge reduction gives 24 sufficient classes from the original 49. This removes redundant obligations. The angle identity then excludes original class 49, leaving 23 open. The complete rule and octahedron theorem remain unproved; the earlier notes are retained below.

title: Four opening positions; 49 simultaneous-failure classes to study
body:
The new octahedron proposal keeps the sharpest apex but allows four positions for the opening at the opposite vertex. An exhaustive combinatorial enumeration reduces simultaneous failure to 49 symmetry classes; none of these new geometric classes is yet excluded.

A comparison on 3,000 sampled shapes found a successful choice throughout. This is numerical evidence only. The earlier single-choice proof still has two gaps, and the seven excluded minus-edge classes remain recorded below.

title: Seven universal failure classes excluded; 21 remain
body:
The new proof step applies Pinciu’s face-neighborhood theorem to one previously residual pair in each tree. It excludes seven of the original 28 simultaneous-failure classes throughout the full convex realization space.

The remaining 21 classes and two-tree conjecture are open. The coordinate-box certificate is unchanged. Targeted numerical searches and exact checks of eight near-flat candidates did not close further classes.

title: Two candidate trees; one now certifies the entire old box
body:
The new two-choice rule switches between two off-quadrilateral stars. Each net consists of two vertex fans. It survived 23,000 discovery shapes and a separate 10,000-shape holdout; its universal validity remains conjectural.

Exact simplification: one of the two trees now covers the whole previously certified ±0.05 box, with 16 closed cells and 336 face-pair checks. The earlier proof used 409 cells and nine trees. The domain has not changed.

Exact examples show that each of the two individual trees can fail, and that all four quadrilateral-only routes can fail together. There is now an exhaustive target of 28 symmetry classes of simultaneous failure; no whole geometric class has yet been excluded. Numerical tests are not proofs.

title: Counts now distinguish proof gaps, local extent, and search coverage
body:
The new dashboard records 4 of 7 types proved, 2 of 3 opposite-petal angle branches proved, and the two remaining octahedron proof obligations. The 19 directly settled face pairs are separated from the four conditional ones.

Minus-edge progress is shown as certified half-widths ±0.01 → ±0.05 in the same ten-coordinate box. The two prism boxes are identified separately: box A is fully certified; box B has only 437/4194304 of its parameter volume marked covered by the search, with full independent replay pending.

A retained before-and-after table makes explicit that the latest research hour closed no universal proof gap. Its exact counterexamples and neighborhood results remain useful, separately recorded progress.

title: Apex-entry failure extends to a certified neighborhood
body:
New exact region: the apex-entry example persists when all eleven free shape coordinates vary independently by ±0.001. Every polyhedron in this closed box satisfies the selection rules, has the apex inside Ω, and still has a certified nonoverlapping net.

This strengthens the counterexample to the individual-apex shortcut. It does not prove the remaining joint-petal claim or Lemma L. The snapshots below retain the earlier discoveries and the prism investigation.

title: Prism route choices narrowed; general theorem still open
body:
Exact negative results: both quadrilateral routes from one fixed degree-four apex can fail. Even at the sharper degree-four apex, the shorter route can fail while the longer one succeeds. The prism section explains these checks.

Numerical lead only: retaining both routes at the sharper degree-four apex survived 60,000 sampled shapes. This does not prove the selection rule. The full n=6 theorem, Lemma L, and the small-fan-angle opposite-petal branch remain open.

The earlier snapshot below records this session’s exact apex-entry counterexample, radial clearance, and axis-nonclosure certificate. The original cone proof and bounded-region certificates remain valid.

title: An individual apex can enter; distances and closure matter
body:
Exactly refuted shortcut: a convex six-vertex example satisfies both selection rules but lets one outer apex enter Ω. All 28 pairs of its net remain nonoverlapping. The full theorem and the joint-petal problem remain open.

New exact checks: the local angular counterexample has a certified radial distance factor of at least 1.217 on every shared direction. A separate five-interval certificate proves that a proposed intrinsic metric cannot close into the prescribed convex octahedron, despite passing all local checks.

The earlier cone proof and 409-region minus-edge cover remain valid. Work continues on distance-sensitive local separation and the joint behavior of the opposite petals.

title: Morning research results · retained snapshot
body:
The full n=6 case remains unproved here. Direct review found an exact counterexample to the DF entry of DiBiase’s displayed octahedron chart. A base-cone proof handles the large-angle and equality branches. Lemma L and the remaining fan-angle sum below π are open.

Independent replay verified a complete 443-region prism-with-one-diagonal certificate and a larger 409-region octahedron-minus-edge certificate. These cover their stated parameter boxes, not whole combinatorial types. A new exact example rules out angular separation around w as a complete proof of Lemma L. Shared-length constraints also ruled out an earlier angle-only candidate. Global coverage remains open.
